1.pericope_label: Then went Samson to Gaza; and at midnight he took the doors of the gate of the city, and the two posts, and carried them up to the top of an hill that is before Hebron

schools.summary: Gill locates Gaza as one of the five principalities of the Philistines, ten miles from Ashkelon, standing on a hill environed with valleys which are themselves enclosed with hills planted with all sorts of delicate fruits, and forty-two miles from the place where Samson was last heard of. What he went there for, Gill says, is not easy to say, but it showed great boldness and courage, after he had made such a slaughter of the Philistines, to venture himself in one of their strongest cities, where he must expect to be exposed to danger; and he thinks it highly probable that this was a long time after the last encounter. The news of his coming he supposes to have been carried to the magistrates either by someone who saw him enter and knew him, or by the woman herself, to whom he had made himself known. On the midnight rising he offers three possibilities: that Samson could not lie longer through the conviction of his conscience for his lewdness, or that he was warned by a dream, or that he had an impulse upon his spirit suggesting the ambush and his danger. He pictures the gate as Samson found it, shut and fast barred and bolted, with the watch perhaps asleep, not expecting his coming until daylight.

Henry treats the opening verse as Samson's sin and refuses to soften it. Taking a Philistine to wife at the beginning of his time was in some degree excusable, but to join himself to a harlot whom he accidentally saw among them was such a profanation of his honour as an Israelite and as a Nazarite that we cannot but blush to read it: tell it not in Gath. This vile impurity, he says, makes the graceful visage of the Nazarite blacker than a coal. He observes that we do not find Samson had any business in Gaza at all, and reports the opinion of some that he went to observe what posture the Philistines were in, so as to gain some advantage against them; but if that was his errand, Henry answers, he forgot it and neglected it. The one comfort he draws from the journey is a thin one: if Samson went to Gaza in quest of such a woman, it would make one willing to hope that, bad as things were otherwise, there were none such among the daughters of Israel.

Keil says Samson went to Gaza in the full consciousness of his superiority in strength to the Philistines, and marks what the text does not say, that unlike the earlier marriage this is not declared to have been of the Lord. On the ambush he notes that the citizens surrounded him and lay in wait all night at the city gate while keeping themselves quiet, meaning to wait until the dawning of the morning and then kill him, and that the verb for it was told has fallen out before their name through a copyist's error. The feat itself he describes as Samson laying hold of the folding wings of the city gate and the two posts, tearing them out of the ground with the bar that fastened them and carrying them to the top of the mountain opposite Hebron; the phrase about Hebron, he insists, means only in the direction towards it and does not place the mountain before the city or in its immediate neighbourhood. Ellicott refuses the side-questions the narrative does not answer, how Samson could venture there in safety, whether he went in disguise, or what his object was, since the narrative is brief and detached. He reads the ambush as a search, since they apparently did not know what house he was in, and takes their quietness as meaning that they made no attack but retired to rest, thinking him secured. He notes the same dropped verb as Keil, presses the verbs of the great act to mean grasping and tearing up, explains the bar as what fastened the two valves together, and observes that Gaza had several gates, so that the smaller gate beside the main one may be meant.

Clarke opens with a summary of the whole chapter and then keeps to physical questions. Of the ambush he says the Philistines shut up all the avenues, secured the gates and set persons in ambush near them, so that they might attack Samson as he left the city early the next morning. Of the carrying off of the gate he reasons backwards from the feat to the scale of the town: though Samson was a very strong man, we do not find that he was a giant, and consequently we may conjecture that the gates of the city were not very large, since he took at once the doors, the two posts and the bar; the cities of those days, he adds, would appear to disadvantage among modern villages. The hill before Hebron he finds a real difficulty, since the city generally understood by that name was about twenty miles distant from Gaza; he offers two ways out, that there were possibly two places called Hebron, or that the phrase is to be understood of the road leading to Hebron, so that Samson carried the gate to the top of the hill that lay on that road.

debates: Whether the visit to Gaza can be explained at all: Henry treats it as bare sin and reports and dismisses the guess that Samson went to reconnoitre, Gill sees boldness and courage in venturing into a strong city, Keil finds the motive in a consciousness of superior strength and notes that the Lord's hand is not claimed here as it was earlier, while Ellicott declares the side-questions unanswerable from so brief and detached a narrative

What the Philistines actually did that night: Clarke has them securing every avenue and posting men in ambush for the morning, while Ellicott supposes they did not know which house he was in, reads the word as going round the city to search, and takes their quietness to mean they had gone to rest

Where the hill stood: Keil says the phrase means no more than in the direction of Hebron, while Clarke, feeling the twenty-mile distance, proposes either a second place of that name or the road leading to Hebron
outliers: Keil and Ellicott independently note that the verb for it was told has dropped out of the text and stands in all the versions
Clarke infers from the feat that the gates cannot have been large, and that the cities of that age would show poorly beside modern villages
Ellicott records the Mohammedan legend of Ali using the gate of Chaibar as a shield, a possible echo of this story
Gill describes Gaza standing on a hill among valleys enclosed by hills planted with delicate fruits

4.pericope_label: He loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah; and the lords of the Philistines said, Entice him, and see wherein his great strength lieth

schools.summary: Gill places the valley half a mile from the brook whence the spies brought back a bunch of grapes as a specimen of the fruit of Canaan, says it seems to have been famous for the best wine, and supposes Samson retired there for refreshment and pleasure; he cites Jerome for a village of a similar name shown in his own day north of Eleutheropolis. The lords he counts as five, having under them the five principalities into which the country was divided, and observes that whether or not their government was united they were united against their common enemy; being great personages, some think they did not come to such a woman's house in person. Delilah he supposes to have chosen a proper opportunity, when Samson was in her caresses, and to have introduced the question in an artful manner, admiring his strange exploits and wondering how he could perform them. The men lying in wait he takes for servants of the lords, placed there privately so that when an opportunity offered they might rush out and fall upon him, whom Josephus calls soldiers.

Henry states the moral of the chapter at its opening. The burnt child dreads the fire, yet Samson, who has more than the strength of a man, in this comes short of the wisdom of a child; for though he had been more than once brought into the highest degree of mischief and danger by the love of women and by lusting after them, he would not take warning, but is here taken in the same snare again, and this third time pays for all. Henry finds the case so exactly described elsewhere that he supposes Solomon to have had this very story in view when, in his caution against uncleanness, he gave his account of the strange woman; and the point he presses is not the strength that failed but the warning that was refused, since the danger had been survived twice already and was entered a third time with open eyes.

Ellicott corrects several things commonly assumed. Delilah was not, as Milton represents, Samson's wife, but, on the authority of Josephus and of the fathers alike, one who played the harlot among the Philistines; nor is it at all clear, though it is generally assumed, that she was a Philistine by race. The place-name he takes as possibly meaning on the brook of Sorek rather than in the valley, the English rendering following the Vulgate, and he notes that Sorek was not in the Philistine district. On the bribe he observes that if she was what Josephus asserts, the Philistine lords could both get access to her and tempt the cupidity of an unprincipled and degraded mind, whereas with a woman of their own race threats would probably have been more effectual. He grants that the narrative, taken as a full account of all that passed, would leave an impression of almost incredible fatuity on Samson's part, judges the ancient versions probably right in reading fresh sinews for the first bonds, dismisses the vine shoots of Josephus as ridiculously inadequate, and takes the seven as the sacred number of perfectness, finding in it a sign that even thus early Samson is playing about on the confines of his secret; the watcher he reads as a single spy sitting in the room to help her. Keil says that after this successful act Samson gave himself up once more to his sensual lusts, glosses the woman's name as the weak or pining one, reckons the offered bribe at eleven hundred shekels from each lord, and counts three deceptions before the truth was told.

Clarke reports the two opinions about Delilah, that some think Samson took her for his wife and others that he had her as a concubine; he holds that she was a Philistine, and remarks that however strong his love for her, she seems to have had none for him, since he always matched improperly and was cursed in all his matches. On the site of the valley he says flatly that it is not easy to be ascertained, quotes the ancient authorities for a position south of Eleutheropolis, and then undercuts them by asking where Eleutheropolis itself was, since ancient writers take all their measurements from places now unknown. He names the five lords by their cities and explains their reasoning: seeing that Samson's stature was not remarkable while his strength was most extraordinary, they supposed it the effect of some charm or amulet, and therefore promised a large sum to learn the secret. The withs he takes for any pliant tough wood twisted into the form of a cord, such as are made of osiers or hazel, comparing the strong ropes made in Ireland from the fibres of bog-wood, while noting that the Greek and Latin versions understood cords made of sinews instead. Of the watchers he observes that they probably never appeared, since Samson broke his bonds the moment the woman cried out.

debates: Who Delilah was: Clarke takes her for a Philistine, whether wife or concubine, while Ellicott denies on the authority of Josephus and the fathers that she was Samson's wife at all and doubts whether she was even a Philistine, and Keil merely names her and glosses the name as the weak or pining one

Where the valley of Sorek lay: Gill and Keil report the ancient identifications with a village near Eleutheropolis, Clarke doubts the whole reckoning by asking where that city itself stood, and Ellicott adds that the word may mean brook rather than valley and that Sorek lay outside Philistine territory

What the first bonds were: Clarke takes them for twisted withs of pliant wood and compares the bog-wood ropes of Ireland, while noting that the versions read sinews; Ellicott judges the versions right, calls the vine shoots of Josephus ridiculously inadequate, and reads the seven as a sacred number betraying how near Samson already was to his secret
outliers: Henry supposes that Solomon had this very story in view in his caution against the strange woman
Ellicott doubts whether more than one spy was hidden in the room, since one could easily be concealed
Clarke notes that the Philistines inferred a charm or amulet from the mismatch between Samson's stature and his strength
Keil reckons the bribe at eleven hundred shekels of silver from each of the five lords

10.pericope_label: Delilah said, Tell me wherewith thou mightest be bound; and Samson deceived her with new ropes, and with the weaving of the seven locks of his head with the web

schools.summary: Gill dates the second attempt from Kimchi, that it was not made on the same day but some time after, when an opportunity offered and Samson was in like circumstances as before, since had she attacked him immediately it might have created a suspicion of the design against him; and the third he places at yet another time, when she thought it most proper to upbraid him with his deception. On the second answer he reports Abarbinel's way of taking the reply, that Samson said he had told her the truth at first and had only forgotten one circumstance, namely that the cords, for so Abarbinel takes the earlier word to mean, should be new and never used. Of Delilah he observes that she tried the experiment according to his directions, being very desirous of getting the sum of money offered her. On the fastening with the pin he leaves the question open, offering three possibilities: that she fastened the beam on which the web was, so that it might not roll back; or her machine or loom to the ground, so that it might stand more firmly; or the web into which the hair was woven, together with the hair itself; and he confesses that which of them is right is difficult to say. He adds that if the addition of the Greek version may be admitted as genuine, supplying some things which seem to be wanting and agreeing best with what follows, the whole becomes plain and easy.

Ellicott supplies the woman's manner between the attempts, that she would of course tell Samson the scene had been merely a playful jest and that she raised the alarm only for the pleasure of one fresh exhibition of his strength, representing her desire to know as loving curiosity. He glosses the old English of the second answer, that occupied means used, and cites the gold occupied for the work of the tabernacle and Ascham's phrase about a new bright silver dish never occupied. Twice he notes how near the answers come to the truth: with the new ropes Samson distantly touches on the consecration which is the secret of his strength, and with the weaving he goes with almost incredible levity and folly to the very verge of it and suffers his sacred hair to be woven in. He corrects Milton's picture of the Nazarite's locks waving and curling about his shoulders, since they were plaited; notes that the word for them occurs here only and is rendered curls and plaits in the Greek; and takes the word for web as technical, perhaps meaning warp. On the loom he presses the terms, that the pin seems to be the wooden peg by which the web was fastened down and the beam is not the weaver's beam of the giant's spear but apparently the comb, the loom being a simple domestic one; and he observes that unless the additions of the Greek and Latin stood in the original text Samson never told her to drive the pin, so that she did it of herself to make assurance doubly sure. Keil counts the second and third deceptions in order and renders the third as a weaving of the seven locks together with the warp.

Clarke reads all three answers as one consistent policy: Samson wished to keep up the opinion which the Philistines already held, that his mighty strength was the effect of some charm, and therefore named seven green withs which had not been dried, new ropes that were never occupied, and the weaving of the seven locks of his hair with the web, since the green withs, the new ropes and the number seven are just such matters as would naturally be expected in a charm or spell. Of the hair he supposes it to have been plaited into seven divisions, and finds a meaning in the number: as the vow of a Nazarite obliged him to wear his hair, and seven was among the Hebrews a number of perfection, the dividing of it into seven locks might more particularly point out the perfection designed by his Nazarite state. He then observes that the verse ends abruptly and does not contain a full sense, reports that Houbigant particularly noticed this and corrected the text from the Greek version, and sets out that version's fuller reading at length.

debates: Whether the text is complete: Clarke says every reader must see that the verse ends abruptly without a full sense and follows Houbigant in correcting it from the Greek, Gill allows that the Greek addition, if genuine, supplies what is wanting and makes the whole plain, while Ellicott draws the consequence that unless the additions were original Samson never told her to drive the pin, so that she did it of herself

What the three answers were meant to do: Clarke takes them as a consistent policy of keeping up the Philistine belief in a charm, since withs, new ropes and the number seven are the stuff of spells, while Ellicott reads them as successive approaches to the truth, each one distantly touching the consecration in which the strength really lay

What was fastened with the pin: Gill offers the beam, the loom itself, or the web with the hair in it, and confesses he cannot decide, while Ellicott identifies the pin as the peg by which the web was held down and the beam as the comb rather than a weaver's beam
outliers: Ellicott corrects Milton, since the Nazarite's locks were plaited and not waving about his shoulders
Clarke finds the seven locks answering to seven as a Hebrew number of perfection, matching the perfection of the Nazarite state
Gill cites Kimchi that the attempts were spaced out lest Samson grow suspicious
Ellicott glosses occupied as an old English word for used, citing Ascham

15.pericope_label: How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me? And he told her all his heart: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me

schools.summary: Gill describes the occasion of the reproach, that Delilah took her opportunity while Samson was caressing her to upbraid him with dissembled love and a false heart, and he identifies the three mockeries she counts as the three answers already given, the binding with green withs, the binding with new ropes, and the weaving of his locks into the web. Of the pressing that followed he says she lay at him day after day to have the secret communicated to her, gave him no rest, and was incessant in her applications. On the disclosure he marks how much further this went than what had gone before: Samson had told her something already, or at least something that came nearer to the truth of the matter, when he directed her to the weaving of his locks into the web, but now he told her all that was in his heart concerning the affair, all that he knew relating to it.

Ellicott observes that Samson had undergone all these wiles before and had experienced their hollowness, and yet had not learnt wisdom by them. The surrender he traces to sheer weariness, rendering the phrase literally as a soul shortened to death, but he refuses to let the weariness excuse it, since even the dangerous use which Delilah had made of his last revelation did not rouse his mind from its besotted stupefaction. He sets the balance of the whole story in a sentence: if Samson thrice proved his vast strength, he also thrice proved his immense folly; to use that strength in the mere saving of his own life was to squander it, and now, as if possessed by insanity, he madly trifles with the key of his secret and risks even the tampering with it. To the same effect he quotes Milton's lines on a man swollen with pride who fell into the snare of fair fallacious looks and laid his head, and the hallowed pledge of all his strength, in the lap of a deceitful woman. Keil notes that Delilah plagued him every day until his soul became impatient even to death, and that the verb used for her pressing occurs nowhere else and signifies in Aramaic to press or plague; on the disclosure he says Samson opened his mind thoroughly to her, telling her that no razor had come upon his head because he was a Nazarite from his mother's womb, and that if he were shaven his strength would depart and he would become weak like all other men.

Clarke is the harshest of them on the disclosure. What a consummate fool, he exclaims, was this strong man; might he not have seen, from what had already taken place, that Delilah intended his ruin? After trifling with her and lying three times, he at last commits to her his fatal secret and so becomes a traitor to himself and to his God. He then borrows a judgment from Calmet which sums up the chapter, that the weakness of Samson's heart in the whole of this history is yet more astonishing than the strength of his body. On the secret itself he supplies the theology the narrative assumes: the miraculous strength of Samson must not be supposed to reside either in his hair or in his muscles, but in that relation in which he stood to God as a Nazarite, such a person being bound by a solemn vow to walk in strict conformity to the laws of his Maker. It was part of the Nazarite's vow to permit no razor to pass upon his head, so that the long hair was the mark of his Nazirate and of his vow to God; and when Samson permitted his hair to be shorn off he renounced and broke that vow, in consequence of which God abandoned him, which is why we are told a little later that the Lord was departed from him.

debates: Why Samson gave way at last: Keil and Ellicott both locate it in sheer weariness, Keil noting the rare verb for Delilah's daily plaguing and Ellicott rendering the phrase as a soul shortened to death, while Clarke refuses weariness as any excuse and calls the disclosure the act of a traitor to himself and to his God

Where the strength really lay: Clarke insists it resided neither in the hair nor in the muscles but in Samson's standing before God as a Nazarite, the hair being only the mark of the vow, so that the shearing was a breach of covenant rather than a loss of a charm; Keil keeps to what Samson himself said, that no razor had come on his head because he was a Nazarite from the womb

How the folly is to be measured: Ellicott balances three proofs of strength against three proofs of folly and calls the spending of that strength on self-preservation a squandering of it, Clarke quotes Calmet that the weakness of the heart is more astonishing than the strength of the body, and Gill marks only how much further this telling went than any before
outliers: Ellicott quotes Milton on the hallowed pledge of all his strength laid in a deceitful lap
Keil notes that the verb for Delilah's pressing occurs nowhere else and is Aramaic for plaguing
Gill observes that Samson had already come nearer the truth when he named the weaving of his locks
Clarke draws the line from the broken vow to the later statement that the Lord was departed from him

18.pericope_label: She made him sleep upon her knees, and caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him

schools.summary: Gill collects the Jewish explanations of how Delilah knew this answer was the true one: she perceived it by his countenance and the serious manner in which he spoke; Abarbinel conjectures that he may have sworn to her that what he said was truth; and the rabbins, with Kimchi, make the proof his naming of God, since in calling himself a Nazarite unto God he used a name she knew he would not take in vain, and his long hair agreed with the account. Of the sleep he supposes that she gave him a sleepy potion, or else encouraged him to take a nap upon her knees and by her fondness lulled him to sleep. Of the seizure he notes that the Philistines only ventured to lay hands on him once Delilah had assured them his strength was gone, of which she had perhaps made trial by binding him and finding he could not free himself until she loosed him; otherwise they would have been afraid. On the last verse he holds that the hair began to grow immediately, as it naturally would, but probably grew in an extraordinary manner and in a short time became as it had been when shaved; not that his strength naturally lay in his hair, but that Samson, being made sensible of his sin and repenting of it, renewed his Nazariteship, of which the letting of the hair grow was the sign.

Henry sets the section under a proverb, that a whore is a deep ditch and that he who is abhorred of the Lord shall fall therein, and says that in that pit Samson sinks. He watches Delilah's management closely, noting what care she took to make sure of the money for herself, since having perceived by the manner of his speaking that he had told her all his heart, she sent for the lords who had hired her on the express condition that they should bring the silver in their hands. Of the last verse he makes the turning point of the whole story: though the last stage of Samson's life was inglorious, and one could wish a veil were drawn over it, the account of his death may be allowed to lessen the reproach, for there was honour in that death. No doubt he greatly repented of his sin and of the dishonour he had done to God, and that God was reconciled to him appears first of all from the return of the sign of his Nazariteship, since his hair began to grow again.

Ellicott says Delilah could not mistake the accent of truthfulness, and that Samson was not so far gone as to be able to reveal the great secret without some sense of awe and shame. Since the locks could hardly have been shaved off without waking him out of any ordinary sleep, he judges that the wording looks as if she had administered some drowsy syrup, and he takes the man she called for to be the concealed spy, quoting Milton on the laying down of Samson's head amid the flatteries of a harlot while he slept and thought no harm. The clause about the Lord's departure he calls deeply tragic, and draws from it that men do not know how much they are changed when the Lord departs from them until they feel the effects of that departure in utter shame and weakness; Samson was under a vow but too weak to resist the current that ran counter to it, particularly once he had come to rely on the mere external sign, for his strength was in no sense in his hair but only in the dedication to God which the hair betokened. On the blinding he prefers the marginal bored out, reports the Arabic gloss that the eyes were burnt out with the red-hot style used for applying stibium, observes that to blind a man was the most effectual humiliation, and compares the tale of Evenius, a priest of the sun-god blinded by the people of Apollonia. Keil takes the man called in to be the spy, so that she need not be alone with Samson, explains the double brass of both hands and both feet being fettered, and finds in the wording of the last verse that Samson lay in captivity only until his hair began visibly to grow.

Clarke reconstructs what the narrative leaves out of the scene: Delilah had probably tied his hands slyly while he was asleep, and after cutting off his hair began to insult him before she called the Philistines, in order to try whether he was really reduced to a state of weakness; finding that he could not disengage himself, she called them, and he, being alarmed, rose up thinking he could exert himself as before. On the blinding he sees the punishment fitted to the sin, since thus the lust of the eye, in looking after and gazing on strange women, was punished; and he adds a reason of policy, that as the Philistines did not know his strength might not return, they put out his eyes so that he might never be able to plan any enterprise against them. The grinding he explains from the state of the art, since before the invention of wind and water mills grain was bruised between two stones and afterwards ground in hand-mills, as is still practised in China and the East, where women and slaves are employed at the work. Of the growing hair he asks whether we may not suppose that, sensible of his sin and folly, Samson renewed his Nazarite vow to the Lord, in consequence of which his supernatural strength was again restored.

debates: How Delilah was satisfied of the truth: Keil rests it on his words and behaviour, Ellicott on the accent of truthfulness and the awe with which Samson spoke, while Gill reports the rabbinic argument that the naming of God was itself the proof, since he would not take that name in vain

Where the strength lay and what the shearing did: Ellicott insists it was in no sense in the hair but in the dedication the hair betokened, and blames Samson for coming to rely on the mere external sign; Gill and Clarke both make the regrowth a token of a renewed vow rather than a natural recovery, Clarke putting it as a question and Gill as a conclusion

What the blinding signifies: Clarke reads it as the lust of the eye punished in kind and adds the captors' policy of making him harmless, while Ellicott treats it as the standard humiliation of a defeated enemy and looks outside Israel for parallels
outliers: Henry sets the whole section under the proverb that a whore is a deep ditch
Ellicott compares the tale of Evenius, a priest of the sun-god blinded by the people of Apollonia
Clarke describes the hand-mills still used in China and the East, where women and slaves are set to grinding
Keil finds in the wording that Samson lay captive only until his hair began visibly to grow

23.pericope_label: The lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god; and they called for Samson, that he may make us sport

schools.summary: Gill dates the gathering some time after Samson's committal to prison, perhaps some months, and takes it to have included the five lords with their friends. When the people saw him in the condition he was in, blinded and fettered, of whom and of whose great exploits they had heard so much, they praised their god as a later king praised his, in hymns and songs composed for the occasion. The merriment he fills in from what was usual: they were merry with wine, for which Gaza is famous in many writers, and with eating and drinking, dancing and music, since it was usual for the heathen to feast in their temples, and especially on such an occasion as this. Of the lad who held Samson by the hand he observes only that nothing is more common now than for a blind man to be led by a boy; and of the crowd, that the house was full of men and women gathered from all parts of the city and perhaps from other places besides.

Henry takes the feast as the point at which the Philistines' own account was closed. Nothing, he says, fills up the sins of any person or people faster than mocking and misusing the servants of God, even though it is by their own folly that they have been brought low. He reads what follows as God putting it into Samson's heart, as a public person, to avenge on them God's quarrel, and Israel's, and his own; and he marks the manner of the recovery, that the strength Samson had lost by sin he recovered by prayer. That the act proceeded not from passion or personal revenge but from a holy zeal for the glory of God and of Israel he infers from God's accepting and answering the prayer, and he insists that the house was pulled down not by the natural strength of the man but by a power given for the occasion.

Ellicott describes the god as upward man and downward fish, points to the later mention of the stump left when the fish-part broke away, derives the name from the word for fish and finds the same root in the name of a Spanish river, and reports the parallel goddess worshipped under the name of Atargatis or Derceto. He gauges how widely the worship spread from the commonness of a place-name compounded with the god's name in the lowlands, and records that the chief temple at Azotus was burned in the Maccabean wars. On the sport he lists the possibilities and declines to choose among them, whether it was by forced jests, or by feats of strength, or merely by being made to submit to insults, citing Josephus that they sent for Samson to insult him over their wine and the Greek version that he played before them while they beat him with rods. On the building he says the temple had a flat roof but that beyond this we are unable to conjecture its architecture, referring the curious to a study of Gaza for an attempt; he observes that different words for men and women are used in the two halves of the verse and infers that the more distinguished people were within with the lords while the common people were on the roof, and he offers the reconstruction of a hall like a Turkish kiosk whose roof rested in front on four columns, two at the ends and two close together in the centre. Keil explains the festival as a celebration of what the Philistines counted a great victory, ascribed by them to their god, and records Samson's request to be let loose to touch the pillars on which the house rested.

Clarke gives the fullest account of the god, quoting Diodorus Siculus that it had the head of a woman while all the rest of the body resembled a fish, noting that the heathens also called the deity Dorceto, and finding the very image described in the lines of Horace about a painter who should join a horse's neck to a human head and let a woman beautiful above end in an ugly black fish. On the sport he says we cannot tell what it was, but thinks it probably an exhibition of Samson's prodigious strength, which the notice of the restored hair seems to intimate, and observes that the exertions he was obliged to make will account for the weariness that gave him his pretence for asking leave to lean against the pillars; he reports the other opinion as well, that Samson was brought out to be a laughing-stock and variously insulted, citing the Greek version that they buffeted him. Of the building he leaves even the kind open, whether it was the prison-house, a house of assembly, or a temple of Dagon, but agrees that it was raised on pillars, open on all sides and flat-roofed, so that it could accommodate a multitude of people on the top.

debates: What the sport was: Clarke inclines to feats of strength, arguing from the notice of the restored hair and from the weariness that gave Samson his pretext, while reporting the view that he was merely a laughing-stock; Ellicott lists forced jests, feats of strength and submission to insult and refuses to decide, citing Josephus and a Greek reading that they beat him with rods

What the building was: Clarke leaves open whether it was the prison-house, a house of assembly or a temple, holding only that it was pillared, open-sided and flat-roofed; Ellicott confines himself to the flat roof, declares the architecture beyond conjecture, and then offers the kiosk with four columns as a possible reconstruction, distinguishing the company within from the crowd above

Where the strength for the final act came from: Henry insists it was not the natural strength of the man but a power given for the occasion, recovered by prayer after being lost by sin, and takes God's answering of the prayer as proof that the motive was zeal rather than personal revenge
outliers: Clarke finds the image of Dagon in Horace's lines on a beautiful woman ending in an ugly black fish
Ellicott derives the god's name from the word for fish and finds the same root in the name of a Spanish river
Gill notes that Gaza is famous in many writers for its wine
Ellicott infers from the two different words for men and women that the notables were inside and the commons on the roof

28.pericope_label: Samson called unto the LORD: O Lord GOD, remember me, and strengthen me only this once; and he bowed himself with all his might, and the house fell upon the lords

schools.summary: Gill raises a question the others pass over, how the prayer came to be recorded. He supposes it made in an ejaculatory manner and mentally, though Samson might possibly have expressed it aloud without being heard amid the noise and mirth, and if it were heard it might only have furnished more ridicule and contempt; from which he concludes that the prayer must have been preserved by the Lord himself and given by inspiration to the writer of the book, since none who heard it lived to relate it to others, not even Samson. On the objection that so large a building could not stand on two pillars set close together in the middle, he answers by accumulating parallels: the architecture of the ancients is little known to us and may have had curious and ingenious arts now lost; Pliny relates two Roman theatres built by Curio which held far more people and were supported on a single pin or hinge; and Westminster hall may be compared. He defends the act itself, that Samson sought their death and was content to lose his own to be avenged, and in neither did he act a criminal part as a judge of Israel, since from a public spirit he might desire his nation's enemies dead, and was the more justified because they were affronting the most high God with their idolatries in the very temple of their idol; his own death he did not simply desire, but was willing to submit to it as the only way of vengeance. Of the burial he thinks it not unlikely that Samson had brothers in the proper sense, since his mother, barren before his birth, might afterwards have had many children.

Ellicott counts three distinct names of God in the address and finds in the petition itself a proof that Samson stood at a comparatively low level of spiritual enlightenment as well as of moral purity; he cannot help feeling that Milton read into the hero's character an austere grandeur which it did not possess, so that the Samson of the poem is rather Milton himself than the Jewish hero, and he describes that stern classic poem as the thundering reverberation of a mighty spirit struck by the plectrum of disappointment. He records a possible rendering of the clause about vengeance, that Samson asks to avenge himself the revenge of one of his two eyes, and prefers the marginal rendering of the next verse, that he leaned himself upon the pillars. Of the burial he supposes Manoah and his wife to have been dead already, and accounts for the unhindered removal of the body by the religious terror which the catastrophe must have caused; and having criticised the poet earlier, he closes by quoting his line that Samson has quit himself like Samson. Keil describes the act, that after praying for strength for this last great deed Samson embraced the two middle pillars on which the building was erected and leant upon them, one with the right hand and one with the left, before bending them with force so that the house fell on the princes and all the people within; and he holds that so far as the fact is concerned there is no ground for questioning its possibility. The blow, he adds, necessarily made a powerful impression on the Philistines, who were plunged into mourning for their princes and for the destruction of the temple of their god.

Clarke uses the prayer to place Samson among the faithful, since it was in consequence of his faith that God would strengthen him to overthrow his enemies and the enemies of his country that he is mentioned among those remarkable for faith. On the two pillars he thinks the learned labour spent on proving that such a building might stand on them has been wasted, since there may have been as many pillars there as in the temple of Diana at Ephesus and yet these two in the centre be the key of the whole, so that once they were pulled down the house must necessarily fall. He reckons the loss carefully: the house was full of men and women with about three thousand of both sexes on the top, and since the whole house was pulled down the principal part of all these were slain, the lords of the Philistines among them; the death of these with so many of the inferior chiefs was such a crush to the Philistine ascendancy that they troubled Israel no more for several years, and did not even attempt to hinder Samson's relatives from taking away and burying his body. He closes on the judgeship, which he finds difficult to date or to measure, since the jurisdiction seems to have been very limited and to have extended no further than the parts of Dan lying next to the land of the Philistines; many suppose that Samson and Eli were contemporaries, Samson being rather an executor of divine justice upon the enemies of his people than an administrator of the civil and religious laws of the Hebrews.

debates: How Samson's last act is to be judged: Clarke and Gill both defend it, Clarke by placing him in the roll of the faithful and Gill by arguing that a judge of Israel might from a public spirit seek his nation's enemies' death, especially in an idol's temple, while Ellicott finds in the very prayer a mark of comparatively low spiritual enlightenment and moral purity

How the objection about the two pillars should be met: Gill answers by accumulating architectural parallels from Pliny and from Westminster hall and by pleading our ignorance of ancient building, whereas Clarke thinks the labour wholly unnecessary, since other pillars may have stood there while these two remained the key of the structure

What Milton has made of the story: Ellicott charges him with reading an austere grandeur into a character that did not possess it, so that the poem's Samson is really Milton himself, and yet closes the chapter by quoting the same poet approvingly on the manner of the hero's death
outliers: Gill argues that the prayer can only have been preserved by inspiration, since no one who heard it survived to report it
Ellicott records a rendering by which Samson asks vengeance for one of his two eyes only
Clarke says the loss of the lords broke Philistine ascendancy for several years and left the burial unopposed
Clarke reports the view that Samson and Eli were contemporaries, the one executing justice while the other administered the law
